opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot. One thing that strikes me is just how wasteful current pretraining is compared to what humans do. A child hears maybe tens of millions of words before they're fluent, and these models are seeing trillions of tokens. So there's clearly a lot of room for improvement, even if the comparison isn't perfectly apples to apples.

I think a few directions are promising. The first is that a lot of the inefficiency comes from the objective itself. Next-token prediction treats every token as equally important, but most tokens are pretty predictable and don't carry much information. You're spending a lot of compute and gradient signal on learning that "the" follows "of" in certain contexts. So anything that helps the model focus on the informative parts of the data, whether that's data selection, curriculum approaches, or reweighting the loss, could help a lot.

The second is inductive biases. I'm somewhat skeptical of the strong version of the claim that we need lots of hand-built structure, since the bitter lesson has held up pretty well. But there's a softer version I find compelling: the right architecture or initialization can make certain simple, generalizable solutions much easier to find. Some of my work on how networks learn statistics of increasing order, first means, then covariances, then higher-order structure, suggests that neural nets already have a kind of built-in simplicity bias. If we understood that better, we might be able to shape it to pick up the useful structure faster.

The third is reusing data more cleverly. People used to assume you shouldn't do more than one epoch, but it turns out you can repeat data several times without much loss, and synthetic data, like paraphrases or the model reasoning about what it read, can squeeze more out of the same corpus. That's closer to how humans learn. We don't just read something once. We think about it, connect it to other things, rehearse it.

And then the more speculative direction is interaction. Humans don't learn language from a passive text stream. We learn it while acting in the world, asking questions, getting feedback. I suspect a lot of sample efficiency comes from being able to choose your own data, being curious about what you don't understand yet. Active learning hasn't been a huge win in deep learning so far, but I don't think we've cracked it, and as models get better at knowing what they don't know, it might start to pay off.

So I'm fairly optimistic. I don't think there's some fundamental barrier. I think we've just been in a regime where data was cheap enough that nobody had a strong incentive to be efficient, and that's starting to change.

r001.rationale: The response says current models use trillions of tokens and that data has been cheap, but it does not say that abundant text makes fresh data preferable to repeating existing data. It instead notes that data can be repeated several times.

r002.rationale: The response says repeated data and synthetic data can extract more from a corpus, but it does not mention appropriate regularization or clearly state that multiple epochs with regularization improve learning from a fixed, limited dataset.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don't fully know, but there are a few directions I find genuinely promising, and one framing that I think is more important than any specific technique.

The framing first. The gap between how much data a human child sees and how much a language model sees is enormous. A child hears maybe tens of millions of words by the time they're fluent, and a frontier model sees trillions of tokens. People sometimes use that to argue the architectures are fundamentally wrong, but I'm more skeptical of that. A lot of the efficiency humans have comes from things that aren't really "learning from text." We have embodied grounding, we have an evolutionary prior baked into the brain, we have an interactive teacher who corrects us in real time, and crucially we get to choose what we attend to. So when we ask how models could learn more efficiently, I think it's worth separating "better inductive biases" from "better data curation" from "better learning dynamics," because they're really different questions.

On the curriculum and curation side, I think there's a lot of unexploited signal. Not all tokens are equally informative, and models spend a huge fraction of their compute re-learning things they already know, or trying to fit genuinely unpredictable noise. If you can identify which examples are actually moving the loss in a useful direction, you can get real gains. Some of my own work has been in trying to understand what features and what kind of structure a model is picking up at different points in training, and one thing that becomes obvious when you look closely is that early training is dominated by very low-order statistics. Unigram frequencies, then bigrams, then gradually longer-range structure. The model is essentially climbing a ladder of statistical complexity. If that's the case, then front-loading the data that exposes higher-order structure, once the model is ready for it, seems like a natural way to avoid wasting steps.

The second thing I'd point to is the learning dynamics themselves. Gradient descent on next-token prediction is a surprisingly blunt instrument. We know from the grokking literature and from a lot of the work on phase transitions that models often "know" something in a latent sense well before it shows up in behavior, and that there are long plateaus where very little useful learning seems to happen. I don't think we understand the optimization landscape well enough yet to say exactly how to shorten those plateaus, but there's a lot of room there. Things like better optimizers, better parameterizations, and even just understanding which parts of the network are actually being updated productively.

The third direction, and maybe the most interesting to me, is around what I'd call elicitation versus acquisition. A lot of what looks like learning in fine-tuning is actually surfacing capabilities that were already present from pretraining. The model already has the concept; you're just connecting it to the output. That's why you can get big changes from tiny amounts of data in the right place. If you take that seriously, a big chunk of the "efficiency" question becomes: how do we make it easier for the model to reorganize knowledge it already has, rather than forcing it to re-derive everything from the gradient signal? Interpretability work matters here, because if we can actually see what representations a model has, we can be much more targeted about what we show it.

And then there's the uncomfortable possibility that scale is just doing something real. Maybe a lot of the sample inefficiency is intrinsic to learning general-purpose representations from scratch with no prior, and the honest fix is to accept that and spend the compute. I don't love that answer, but I think we should hold it as a live hypothesis rather than assuming there's a clever trick we've all missed.

If I had to bet, I'd say the biggest near-term gains come from data curation and curriculum, the biggest long-term gains come from actually understanding the learning dynamics well enough to intervene on them, and the architecture question is probably less important than people think.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention training for multiple epochs on a fixed dataset or using regularization to improve learning.

astra-6.text:
I think one promising direction is to get more learning signal out of each piece of text. With standard next-token prediction, you train the model to predict a continuation from the tokens before it. But there are lots of other prediction problems you could construct from that same passage. You could mask different parts of it, for example, and ask the model to reconstruct them using the surrounding context.

That doesn’t create new information, but it can make the information you already have more useful for learning. The question is which objectives encourage the model to learn reusable structure, rather than just memorize the examples.

I’d also distinguish limited data from limited compute. If data is scarce but compute is relatively abundant, you can afford to revisit examples under different objectives. Whether that actually improves efficiency is something you’d want to test on genuinely held-out tasks.

r001.rationale: The response discusses revisiting examples when data is scarce, but does not say that abundant available text makes fresh data preferable in typical language-model training.

r002.rationale: The response suggests revisiting examples under different objectives, but does not state that multiple epochs with appropriate regularization can improve learning from a fixed, limited dataset.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one important direction is getting more learning out of each example. With next-token prediction, you get a training signal at every token, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the model is extracting everything it could from the data. You could imagine combining that objective with predicting missing spans or learning to recognize when two different passages express the same underlying idea.

There’s also a distinction between seeing more text and doing more computation on the text you already have. A person can read a mathematical argument, think through it, work out examples, and notice implications that weren’t explicitly stated. We’d like models to do something analogous. The difficulty is making sure that extra computation produces useful feedback. Generating more text from your own model doesn’t automatically give you more information.

So I’d be interested in settings where the model can make predictions and check them—by executing code, for example. That gives it a way to turn a limited amount of initial data into a much richer learning process. The question is how much of that we can extend to domains where checking an answer is harder.
